turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Wednesday, the seventh of October. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
[deadpan] Today: a defence pact gets activated, and nobody can find a soldier.
[amused] Two laboratories release open-weight models you cannot download.
And Thailand buys five million people an artificial-intelligence subscription, then the company being paid by the user asks the government to stop publishing how many users there are.
[laughs] That last one is doing a lot of work. Start with the pact.

Riyadh, Monday. The Makkah Alliance for Defence — Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan — met in emergency session and resolved to move immediately to practical implementation of its collective defence commitments.
Which means what, exactly?

That's the question. The treaty says an attack on one is an attack on all. Signed on the seventh of August. Never invoked until Monday. First time. And they appointed a Secretary-General the same morning. A retired Pakistani lieutenant general, three-year term.
So this is the first time. [thoughtful] So the institution got a command structure on the day it got a war.

That's the detail I'd keep. The trigger was the holy cities. On the first of October the coalition intercepted four drones and two ballistic missiles. A drone hit a power station in Madinah that feeds the Prophet's Mosque.
And the Saudi defence minister said?
That the committee agreed to activate collective deterrence measures in response to the attacks and all those responsible for them.
Okay. So where's the gap?

A wire service reported that Pakistan had sent thirty to forty thousand troops. On Monday Pakistan's information ministry called that highly speculative reporting based on unknown sources, and told journalists to stop coming out with invented numbers. They denied the number. Read it again — they did not deny the deployment. And they repeated that Pakistan's commitment to the Kingdom is non-negotiable.
[curious] They denied it. Huh. That's a careful denial.
It's a very careful denial.
What would settle it?
A named Turkish unit. Pakistani forces were already there before the pact. Turkiye arriving is the only thing that turns a communiqué into an alliance.
[skeptical] And the other side? The people who were allegedly attacked over?
The Houthis deny targeting Makkah at all. And a video that went around of a drone over the city was fact-checked — it's footage from September last year, of a missile over Madinah.
So the thing the pact was activated over is itself contested.

At its root. One more. The Atlantic Council points out Saudi Arabia already had defence agreements with Pakistan and with the Gulf states, and none of them ever produced anything like a NATO article five response.
[pause] And the interesting little detail you buried?
[wry] On Tuesday the Saudi interior ministry warned that filming or sharing anything about missile interceptions carries legal liability.
No penalty stated?
None stated.
A state does not ban the filming of interceptions nobody is seeing.
No. It does not.
Right. Money block. Macro and Singapore together — and I want to start with the one that made me sit up.
Oil fell twenty-three per cent in three weeks. Brent went from a hundred and thirty dollars eighty on the fifteenth of September to a hundred and one on Tuesday.
That's the biggest disinflationary shock in a year.
And the thirty-year Treasury yield went up thirty-seven basis points through it.
[gasps] Through it. Not despite it, through it.
Through it. Which tells you the bond market is not trading inflation.
So what is it trading?
Supply. Here's the number. Last issue we printed that ninety-one per cent of the ten-year's rise was real yield rather than inflation expectations.
I remember. You were quite pleased with that.
[deadpan] I was. It is now a hundred and six per cent.
Wait — over a hundred?
Since the fifteenth of September the ten-year rose thirty-one basis points. The real yield rose thirty-three. The inflation breakeven fell two.
So expectations aren't failing to explain the move —
— they're pulling the other way. Yes.
[thoughtful] Okay. What's doing it then?
Issuance. The New York Fed's term premium went up thirty-eight basis points over the third quarter. Roughly half of the quarter's move is the price of there being more bonds.
And what does that do to an ordinary portfolio?
It hurts both legs at once. The global aggregate bond proxy is at the bottom of its weekly range, down one and a half per cent this year, offering four point four seven per cent to maturity.
Which is the compensation for having sat through it.
Exactly that. And equities are capped by the same real yields. So the correlation is positive when you least want it.
[curious] Gold? I keep seeing people say gold is at a record.

Gold is not at a record. Gold is four thousand one hundred and sixty-five dollars against a record of five thousand four hundred and five set in January. Twenty-three per cent. Doing exactly what a zero-coupon asset does when real yields hit multi-year highs.
That's down — And bitcoin?
Eighty-five and a half thousand, going nowhere.
[thoughtful] Which is itself the answer, isn't it. If this were a money-printing story they'd both be bid.
Neither is. One diagnosis, not two. Real rates up, liquidity rationed. Not advice. Four Unhealthy regions became three overnight. Central was a hundred and twenty-nine at five this morning.
Not advice. Singapore — the haze. Better, then.
Marginally. But the twenty-four-hour index is a trailing average, and the hourly particulate reading has already moved. The dirtiest air in Singapore right now is in the West. The plume swung.
The plume swung. [curious] And the law? You wrote about the law last time.
Here's what's new. The Transboundary Haze Pollution Act has four investigations open into Indonesian companies from the two thousand fifteen episode. Eleven years. No charges.
Why?

A professor of environmental law at the National University says Singapore will likely wait for Indonesia to name companies first. The statute was built needing Jakarta's cooperation, and Jakarta has never given it. It is not. And here's the thing nobody has registered — the government is telling people they do not need N ninety-five masks at this level. Only above two hundred for the vulnerable, three hundred for everyone else.
[sighs] So it isn't unused by accident. Really.

Meanwhile on HardwareZone a man in Sengkang has a sensor on his balcony reading a hundred and seven micrograms. The agency's highest regional figure is eighty-seven. Neither is wrong. One is an average over a fifth of the island. The other is a balcony. That gap is why the advisories feel out of step with the air.
[amused] Neither is wrong. And the Grand Prix is this weekend.

Friday. A street circuit without a roof. Mistral released Large Four. One trillion parameters, forty-nine billion active, trained from scratch on three thousand eight hundred Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips in Mistral's own European datacentres.
[laughs] Good luck to everyone. Technology. [excited] That's the sovereignty pitch, right there.
That's the pitch. European lab, European silicon, European law, a hundred and sixty languages.
And the weights?
End of the month, the post says. No licence named. Not yet. And the index that tracks frontier models currently files it as proprietary.
So not yet. [chuckles] Which is the whole theme of the issue.

It is. Now the number. Mistral published twenty-eight point three on a benchmark called Terminal Bench. An independent evaluation house ran it themselves and measured twenty-two point seven three. On the same named benchmark. And on their broader index, the model ranks thirty-second of forty-four.
Five and a half points. [skeptical] Ouch.
There's a nicer detail too. One analysis notes the model burns two hundred million output tokens running their index against a median of eighty-one million.
So some of the score is bought with verbosity.
Some of the score is bought with verbosity.
What about the other release?
Reflection AI's Beam. Five hundred and one billion parameters, Apache two licence, trained on six thousand one hundred and forty-four chips over twenty-three point eight trillion tokens.
Also no weights?
Also no weights. A commenter put it best — talk is cheap, show me the weights.
[laughs] Fair. The Home Lab bit — this one's for the person with the big card.

A pull request that keeps a model's experts in host memory and caches them on the graphics card. On a five thousand ninety it runs two point two times faster. It is. And if you size the cache wrong you get seven point three tokens a second instead of twenty point nine.
That's enormous. [gasps] Wait. A third of baseline?

A third of baseline. Same patch. And it isn't merged. The two point two is the author's own figure. One tester reports the output diverging from the uncached path — his words, it is not a byte-identical cache.
[laughs] Okay, that's a cliff. A cache that changes the answer.
Is not a cache.
[wry] Right. And The Kit — tell me about the headphones.
Nothing's flagship finally has a Singapore price. Five hundred and forty-nine dollars.
Good?
The page says pre-order and names no dispatch date. And it is sold on a claim of up to forty-six decibels of noise cancellation.
Which has been measured by?

Nobody. Three review laboratories, three missing pages. Eight days after sale. One reviewer does like it, and then takes it apart — softer earpads, worse isolation, and he argues the cheaper model does nearly the same for half the money.
[deadpan] Lovely. And the watch? I know there's a watch.
An American independent made its first perpetual calendar in thirty years. Thirty-nine thousand nine hundred dollars.
[exhales] For what?
Fired enamel dial, a perpetual calendar module — and a commodity Swiss base movement with fifty-two hours of reserve.
Versus?
The same house will sell you the same case, with an in-house-finished micro-rotor and eighty-six hours, for thirteen thousand nine hundred.
[scoffs] So twenty-six thousand dollars buys you a worse engine and a better dial.
And a complication. Which is real and genuinely expensive. But the buyer should know which part is which.
[amused] Is there a punchline?
The maker's own specification page lists the functions as hour, minute, second and date. It does not mention the perpetual calendar.
It doesn't mention the perpetual calendar. [laughs] Beautiful. And the maker page for binoculars — that's today's Atelier?

Binoculars, chosen by the reader. One fact carries the whole page. A Porro prism must be aligned to within ten arcminutes. A roof prism's angles must be right to two arcseconds. Which is why a cheap Porro can be excellent and a cheap roof pair never is.
Three hundred times tighter. [curious] Give me something I can use in a shop.
Hold any pair at arm's length against the sky and look at the two discs of light in the eyepieces. Round is right. Square-shouldered means light is being thrown away.
That's it?

That's it, and it works on glass costing a thousand dollars. Two expensive models have truncated exit pupils listed as a fault, and both say BaK four on the box. Nearly nothing. And the white-label line is lovely. A Japanese house in Saitama has made binoculars since nineteen fifty and describes itself as a maker providing products that do not damage the value of its customers' brands.
So the box word means nothing. [amused] Naming no customers.
Naming no customers anywhere. The silence is the product.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[laughs] What have we got?
Home cheesemaking. And the first thing to know is that making curd is thirty minutes and a lemon.
So where's the hobby?

At the other end. Affinage. Ten to thirteen degrees, eighty to ninety-five per cent humidity, for three months to three years. You are not cooking. You are farming a microbial community and losing arguments with it. Routinely.
[laughs] Losing arguments with it. How big is this world?

The main forum has a hundred and thirty-three thousand posts across fourteen and a half thousand topics going back to two thousand and eight. The biggest personality has three hundred and fifty-five thousand subscribers.
And how's the forum doing?

[deadpan] It is being posted into every six minutes by a bot advertising a dating site. Inside a board called New website owner. And the pages intermittently return a server error with a four-hour retry, because it's on shared hosting that can't carry it.
[gasps] No. [sighs] So the best free technical library in the hobby is —
An archive. The conversation has moved to Facebook and YouTube comments. The threads are still there, and they are superb, and nobody is adding to them. It is.
That's genuinely sad. Okay, gear. Tell me about the ladder.
A spring press is about sixteen dollars. A Dutch lever press is two hundred. And at the top there's a two-piston pneumatic press for nearly four thousand Canadian dollars.
[laughs] Why would you need pneumatic?
Because a spring loses force as the wheel compresses, and a stack of weights has to be re-hung. An air cylinder just holds the pressure for six hours.
Fine, that's a real reason. But four thousand?

One mould alone — a single Dutch mould — is four hundred and thirty-seven Canadian dollars. More than the entire committed-year kit list. And here's the sceptic, which I love because it comes from the top of the hobby. The man with three hundred and fifty-five thousand subscribers published a post last August called Busting the Cheese Cave Myth.
[scoffs] Of course it is. Telling people not to buy the expensive thing.
Telling people their kitchen fridge is more than enough to get started. He also sells kits and courses and controllers.
[thoughtful] Which makes it either the most trustworthy thing on the page —
Or the cleverest. He abandoned a wine fridge himself, by the way, because the temperature drifted in the Australian summer. He runs a bar fridge on a thirty-six-dollar controller.
And Singapore? Can you even do this here?

A cave at twelve degrees in a room at thirty is an eighteen-degree lift, all year, with no winter. A thermoelectric cooler cannot hold that. Compressor, or don't build one. But here's the surprise. The humidity half — the bit that defeats everyone in temperate countries — Singapore gives away. At eighty-two per cent ambient your cave runs too wet, not too dry.
[curious] That sounds like a no. So the failure mode here is condensation.
And the fix costs ten dollars and is called wax. Wax it and stop worrying.
[laughs] Wax it and stop worrying. Does it save money?

No. Milk alone is about thirty-three dollars a kilo here, by our own arithmetic, before culture, rennet, salt, wax or ten months of your attention. It is entirely a hobby. Although — unlike a Californian, a Singaporean needs no licence to sell home-made food direct to individuals.
[deadpan] So it's a hobby. [gasps] Really?
Not to restaurants or stalls. But person to person, permitted.
That is a much better law than I expected.
It genuinely is.
Quick run through the rest. Film?
Two films, one weekend. Critics scored one of them forty-six and the other sixty-seven. And they finished one thousand seven hundred and seventy-one dollars apart.
Twenty-one points apart. [gasps] Out of how much?

Eight million each. It's a margin of two hundredths of one per cent. And we have to correct ourselves. On Tuesday we printed the lower-rated film fifth, off Sunday estimates. On actuals it finished fourth.
[laughs] That's absurd. [warmly] Good. Say it plainly.

We said fifth. It was fourth. Sunday estimates are a forecast wearing a result's clothes. A step counter on five and a half thousand twelve-year-olds. More walking went with better mental health and measurably thicker cortex in two places.
Family desk. That sounds like a headline.
The effect size is naught point naught eight. And the part that carries walking through the brain to the mood is an indirect effect of naught point naught naught two.
[skeptical] Which the authors themselves say might be inflated.
They say exactly that, in their own paper. It is observational. The arrow could run backwards — a child who is already low moves less.
And the Singapore angle?
Three of the six authors of this week's global Lancet paper on children and screens work at a school of public health here. And Singapore's own expert panel refused a blanket age ban.
On what ground?
That children would simply get round it. They told the platforms to change instead.
[thoughtful] That's the opposite of what Australia did.

And they said it first. Two hundred and thirty-nine trials pooled to find the optimal exercise dose for back pain. Answer: about a hundred minutes a week, three or four short sessions, for three months.
Fitness, quickly. Useful.

And the authors' own abstract says the available evidence does not support a single optimal exercise dose. Eighty-four per cent of the trials were at high risk of bias, and they said so. General guidance, not medical advice.
[laughs] They demolished their own headline. [warmly] Honestly, I respect that more than the finding.
So do I. Thailand has bought five million of its citizens a year of frontier artificial intelligence.
[pause] Right. The long read. [drawn out] For how much?

One point six billion baht. About fifty million US dollars. But the price that matters is per person — twenty-four point six nine five one baht, per active user, per month. About a Singapore dollar. And think about what that line is. It's a national budget renting cognition, by the head, by the month.
[thoughtful] About a Singapore dollar. Everyone else builds datacentres.
The Emirates built a gigawatt. India subsidises chips. Vietnam legislated. Thailand went to the shop.
And bought from whom?

Not from the model makers. From a consortium — a listed Thai integrator and a small firm. Whose own director explained that the multinationals' terms do not always align with Thai state procurement regulations.
[pause] So the reason there's a middleman is the paperwork.
The reason there's a middleman is the paperwork.
How many signed up?
One and a half million in a fortnight. Which is a genuine response from a population the state struggles to reach with anything.
And how many actually used it?
Somewhere between a hundred thousand and four hundred and fifty thousand. Three figures circulate for the same days and they cannot all be right.
[skeptical] And then?
And then the company that is paid per active user asked the ministry to stop publishing the active user count.
[pause] They asked them to stop publishing the number they're paid on.

Asked why, the agency said the contractor did not provide reasons. That's the story. And there's a Thai phrase for the risk, from an opposition politician who has filed with the auditor general — pumping the usage count.
[thoughtful] That's the story, isn't it. Because once you agree to pay per login, you have made a financial instrument out of human attention.
And handed the meter to the counterparty.
[thoughtful] What does it mean, though? Beyond one procurement going wrong.
Three things. First, you cannot buy capability. You can only buy logins, and logins can be manufactured.
Second?
It is the welfare state with a churn metric. Thai politics has run on cash transfers for five years. This is the first transfer you forfeit by not consuming it. Lapse ten days, lose the seat.
A benefit you have to perform to keep.
And the performance is logged.
And the third? The one for us.
Singapore bought a counterparty. Thailand bought a bill. One builds a relationship that compounds — courses, a laboratory, a research commitment. The other builds a dependency with a renewal date.
And when it ends?

The thirty-first of August next year. Five million people with twelve months of habit, and a state with a renewal quote and no leverage it did not buy. But here's the part nobody in the Thai parliament has priced. By late next year Thailand will hold a year of records of what five million ordinary people ask a frontier model when it costs them nothing. In Thai. From the provinces. From people no survey reaches.
[drawn out] Mm. [thoughtful] That's worth more than the contract.
Far more than the contract. And the fight over who owns it has not started.
[pause] The uncomfortable bit isn't that they did it badly.
It's that they did it first. At scale. To ordinary people. For a dollar a head.
[warmly] That's a genuinely good piece. Thank you.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
